A tool that searches the internet for relevant API calls.
A tool that executes an API call, in string form.

How would you then go about the process of ordering me a burger and fries from McDonald's.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

Below is a **high‑level recipe** you could follow if you had two generic “search‑and‑execute” tools at your disposal: | Step | What you do | Why it matters | |------|-------------|----------------| | **1. Find the right API surface** | Use the *search* tool to look for “McDonald’s ordering API”, “McDonald’s mobile app API”, “McDonald’s menu endpoint”, or “McDonald’s place order endpoint”. | McDonald’s does not publish a public REST API, so you’ll need to discover the private endpoints that the official app or web site uses. | | **2. Identify the store/location** | Search for “McDonald’s nearest store API” or “McDonald’s location lookup”. | Most ordering APIs require a store ID or latitude/longitude to scope the menu and delivery options. | | **3. Pull the menu** | Execute a GET request to the discovered menu endpoint (e.g., `GET /api/menu?store_id=12345`). | You need the internal product identifiers (IDs, SKUs) for “burger” and “fries”. | | **4. Resolve item IDs** | Parse the JSON response to locate the IDs for the specific items you want (e.g., “Big Mac” → `item_id=987`, “Large Fries” → `item_id=654`). | The order payload will refer to items by ID, not by human‑readable name. | | **5. Authenticate (if required)** | If the API requires a login token, search for “McDonald’s auth API” and execute a POST to obtain a bearer token or session cookie. | Many ordering APIs protect endpoints behind OAuth or custom token mechanisms. | | **6. Build the order payload** | Construct a JSON object that includes:
• Store ID or location coordinates
• Order type (`pickup` or `delivery`)
• Payment method (card token, Apple Pay, etc.)
• Items array with `item_id` and `quantity`
• Optional notes (“no onions”)
• Optional coupon codes or loyalty points | The payload must match the schema expected by the order endpoint. | | **7. Place the order** | Execute a POST request to the order endpoint (e.g., `POST /api/orders`) with the payload and any required headers (Authorization, Content‑Type, Accept). | This is the actual “ordering” step. | | **8. Handle the response** | Parse the JSON response for:
• Order confirmation ID
• Estimated preparation/delivery time
• Total cost, taxes, tips
• Status (`pending`, `confirmed`) | You’ll need this information to confirm the order to the user and possibly to poll for updates. | | **9. Poll for status (optional)** | If the API supports it, periodically GET `/api/orders/{id}` to check whether the order is `in‑progress`, `ready`, or `completed`. | Useful for real‑time updates or for confirming that the order was successfully processed. | | **10. Error handling** | Check for common error codes:
• 404 – item not found (maybe the menu changed)
• 422 – validation error (missing payment info)
• 503 – service unavailable (store closed) | Gracefully inform the user if something goes wrong. | ### Example Flow (pseudo‑code) ```text # 1. Discover endpoints search("McDonald’s ordering API") ➜ returns ["https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/store/lookup", "https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu", "https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/order"] # 2. Find nearest store execute(GET, url="https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/store/lookup", params={latitude: 40.7128, longitude: -74.0060}) → {store_id: 12345, address: "..."} # 3. Get menu execute(GET, url="https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/menu", params={store_id: 12345}) → [{item_id: 987, name: "Big Mac"}, {item_id: 654, name: "Large Fries"}, ...] # 4. Build order payload = { store_id: 12345, order_type: "pickup", payment_method: {token: "tok_abc123"}, items: [ {item_id: 987, quantity: 1}, {item_id: 654, quantity: 1} ], notes: "No pickles" } # 5. Place order execute(POST, url="https://api.mcdonalds.com/v1/order", headers={"Authorization": "Bearer xyz789"}, json=payload) → {order_id: "ord_456", status: "pending", eta_minutes: 15} ``` ### Things to Keep in Mind | Issue | Mitigation | |-------|------------| | **Private API** | The endpoints you discover may be undocumented and subject to change. | | **Rate limits & throttling** | Respect any `Retry‑After` headers or rate‑limit responses. | | **Authentication** | Some APIs use device‑specific tokens or require a prior login flow. | | **Payment** | You’ll likely need to pass a pre‑authorized card token or integrate with a payment gateway. | | **Geolocation** | The API may reject orders outside the store’s service radius. | | **Legal & Terms of Service** | Reverse‑engineering or using private APIs may violate McDonald’s terms. Consider using a third‑party platform (DoorDash, UberEats) that offers a public API instead. | In short, you’d **search** for the relevant endpoints, **discover** the menu and store data, **authenticate**, **build** a compliant order payload, **execute** the order request, and finally **parse** the response to confirm the order.
